job: Power steering fluid service (drain and refill or exchange)
unit: per vehicle with hydraulic power steering: replacing the power steering fluid by draining and refilling through the reservoir or return hose, or by a simple exchange, then bleeding the air out. Parts are the fluid only (five 12-ounce bottles on the Honda and Acura examples, three quarts on the truck). Not included: cleaning chemicals or additives, a pump, hoses, rack or gear, belt, leak diagnosis or leak repair. Vehicles with electric power steering have no fluid and do not need this service

finding: The site has no live range for this job, so there is nothing to grade; these are first figures. This service applies only to vehicles with hydraulic power steering; most newer cars have electric power steering and no fluid, which is why the examples are older. Shops usually sell it at a set menu price, not as parts plus clocked labor. Built totals (fluid + stated hours x $120-$160/hr, the national middle labor rate used for these checks): economy 2007 Honda Civic about $100-$210, midsize 2003 Honda Accord about $100-$210 and luxury 2010 Acura MDX about $100-$210 (five 12-ounce bottles of genuine Honda or Acura fluid at $8.00-$10.00 each, 0.5-1.0 hr); truck 2010 Chevrolet Silverado 1500 about $168-$220 (3 quarts of GM power steering fluid at $19.97, 0.9-1.0 hr). A fair plain-language range is roughly $100-$220. Against the benchmarks: FIXD ($95-$125) sits at the low end, and YourMechanic ($168-$212) and Sunbit ($170-$205) sit in the upper half; all three fall inside or touch the built range. How solid the figures are, stated plainly. Labor: the truck low end is the one manufacturer time found, GM's 0.9 hr 'Flush and Bleed Power Steering System', which covers the 2007-2014 Silverado 1500 by name; it is a warranty time for a cold-weather noise repair, printed unchanged in five revisions of the bulletin. No Honda or Acura time for this job was found, so the three car classes rest on one technician's statement in a February 2000 trade article that a Honda flush takes him about half an hour (low) and one regional chain's statement that a flush can take up to 1 hour (high); neither is a flat-rate book time or for the example vehicle, and two do-it-yourself guides say 1 to 2 hours. Fluid quantity is the weakest part: owner's manuals for these vehicles print the fluid type but no power steering capacity, and no maker document stating a service-fill quantity for any example was loaded. The Honda and Acura quantity (five bottles) comes from that same trade article, which names neither the model nor the bottle size (12 ounces is assumed because that is the size the fluid is sold in); the truck quantity (3 quarts) comes from a GM bulletin for a different GM vehicle and fluid. A simple reservoir drain and refill uses less fluid than these figures and a machine exchange can use more. Prices: the Honda and Acura figures are the genuine fluid at a dealer's list and discounted price, because no aftermarket fluid stated to meet the Honda specification loaded with a price; the truck has a single GM list price, so its parts low and high are the same. The Civic manual page does not print the model name or year (2007 Civic by its file name) and the Accord page does not either (2003 by its publication code). An estimate is not a quote. Posted menu prices loaded on 2026-11-20 from six sellers' own pages (three dealers, one regional chain and two local multi-shop independents in Michigan, West Virginia, New Jersey, Ohio, Pennsylvania, North Carolina and Georgia) run from $69.99 to $207.88 for the whole car, mostly before tax and shop fees: $69.99-$99.99 at the Michigan independent, $79.95 and $99.00 at two dealers, $99.99 at the chain (a chemical-cleaner flush, marked as a different service), $158.99 at the North Carolina independent and $207.88 at a Honda dealer; national chains were not searched because they do not print this price. Held (2026-11-20, first attempt, reviewer): no maker document states how much fluid the service takes for any example. The Honda and Acura quantity is five bottles from a 2000 trade article that names neither the model nor the bottle size, and the truck quantity is from a bulletin for different vehicles with a different fluid, so the parts figures rest on an assumption. Hours and six posted prices are saved.
extras: A quote often adds shop supplies, fluid disposal and sales tax. Many shops sell a machine exchange with a cleaning chemical or a conditioner additive instead of a plain drain and refill, which costs more. If the visit is for a whine, stiff steering or a leak, expect a separate diagnosis fee, and a leaking hose, pump, rack or steering gear or a worn belt is quoted separately. Some vehicles need a specific fluid (Honda and Acura fluid, a synthetic fluid such as Pentosin on many European cars and cold-climate GM trucks, or automatic transmission fluid on others), and the wrong one can damage seals. Vehicles with electric power steering do not need this service at all.
